chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, from Musa ibn Umar, from Ja'far ibn Basheer, from Ibrahim ibn Mihzam, from Abu Maryam, from Al-Asbagh ibn Nubata, who said:

I entered upon the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him), and in front of him was grilled meat. He said to me, 'Approach and eat.' I said, 'O Commander of the Faithful, this is harmful to me.' He said to me, 'Approach. I will teach you some words with which nothing from what you fear will harm you. Say: In the Name of Allah, the Best of Names, filling the earth and the sky, the Beneficent, the Merciful, He with Whose Name nothing harms and no illness [comes]. Have lunch with us.'

key_terms.أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ: Commander of the Faithful (Title for Imam Ali)
key_terms.مِلْءَ الْأَرْضِ وَ السَّمَاءِ: Filling the earth and the sky

ai.seo_question: What supplication did Imam Ali teach to protect against harm from food?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam Ali (peace be upon him) instructs Al-Asbagh ibn Nubata to recite a specific dhikr before consuming grilled meat, addressing the pre-Islamic and early Islamic concern that certain foods might cause harm or illness. The supplication emphasizes the protective power of Allah's Name, asserting that nothing causes harm when accompanied by His name, thereby transforming a mundane act of eating into a spiritual remedy. This reflects the Shia tradition of using divine names as a means of seeking protection (ta'awwud) and ensuring the purity of sustenance.
